### Asia Sells the Chip Stocks for a Second Day Ahead of Nvidia's Report After the Close, the President Flies Into Manila for the Quad's First Meeting in Two Years, and Alaska's Count Stands at 141,637 to 130,162 With Ms. Peltola 52 Votes From a Majority and One Day of Mail Left

Filed as: Edition No. 58 — The Overnight Watch · 2026-11-17T04:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-17-overnight-watch.html

The Night File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Asia Sells the Chip Stocks for a Second Day Ahead of Nvidia’s Report After the Close, the President Flies Into Manila for the Quad’s First Meeting in Two Years, and Alaska’s Count Stands at 141,637 to 130,162 With Ms. Peltola 52 Votes From a Majority and One Day of Mail Left

 The night file: a second Asian session sold the chipmakers from Seoul to Taipei ahead of the one report the week waits on; a petition counted at 188,548 in the evening against a board reported by named and unnamed voices not weighing a return; a president in the air to Manila and a premier already heard there; a strike day opening in France on the movement’s eighth anniversary; a tanker named off Oman against six sunk in a claim and none confirmed; and a Senate count that did not move in the night, with Tuesday’s mail the next fact.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Tuesday, November 17, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 57, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, from Edition No. 56, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Monday, from Edition No. 55, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Monday, and from Edition No. 54, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Monday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the overnight figures differ from the earlier figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Night in Brief: A Second Selling Day, a Petition Past 188,000, and No Count Moved

The night sold the chip stocks a second day, counted a petition past 188,000 names, and moved no count and no board. Asia’s Tuesday session followed Wall Street’s correction lower, Seoul’s Kospi closing down 2.6 percent to 4,968.48 in the Press account filed below, ahead of the one report the week waits on: Nvidia’s third-quarter results after Tuesday’s close, the first since Mr. Huang’s resignation, with consensus revenue at about $109 billion. The petition for his return was read at 188,548 names on Monday evening in the petition account filed below, against a board reported to be focused on its investigation and not in talks about a return. The President flies into Manila late Tuesday afternoon for the Quad’s first leaders’ meeting in two years, in the wire account filed below, with Thursday’s room in Shenzhen behind it. Alaska’s count did not move in the night: it stands at 141,637 to 130,162, Ms. Peltola 52 votes short of a majority on the current total, with about 6,500 ballots estimated still to count, in the Juneau account filed below. In the Gulf, a tanker has been named off Oman against six sunk in a claim. In France, a strike day opens. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the night settled is short: the selling is a second day and not a turn, the board’s reported position hardened without the board speaking, and every dated thing on Tuesday’s calendar—retail sales at 0830, the Secretary’s lunch, the Quad at 1830 in Manila, the count in Juneau, the report after the close—still stands where Monday left it. What it left open is the rest of the file: the call, the numbers, the radar, and the room.

The Count at 0400: 141,637 to 130,162 Stands, 52 Votes to the Line, and Tuesday’s Mail Is the Next Fact

Alaska’s count spent the night where Monday afternoon left it, and the overnight file adds three readings of the same numbers and one statement. The Press’s count as of 0252 UTC on Tuesday prints the state’s Monday figures at a rounded 50.0 percent for Ms. Peltola—141,637 votes to Senator Sullivan’s 130,162, on 283,377 votes in the contest, with about 98 percent estimated counted—and the Press has not called the race, in the Press count account filed below. On the full denominator the share is 49.98 percent, and a majority on the current total is 141,689, leaving her 52 votes short, in the Juneau account above. NBC News estimates about 6,500 ballots remain to be counted, in the same account; more ballots arriving by mail will be counted on Tuesday, and overseas ballots may arrive through Wednesday.

The other side has now said how it will wait. Senator Sullivan’s spokesman, Mr. Adams, said on Monday night that Alaskans deserve a complete and accurate count, that the campaign will let the process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified, and that it will not comment on individual ballot updates or outside projections in the meantime; the campaign will have more to say by the end of the week, in the Juneau account. One outside projection stands in the file as a model and nothing more: a newspaper’s independent tabulation of the Division’s scanned ballot record, covering 282,698 ballots, puts Ms. Peltola ahead 143,127 to 132,985, or 51.83 percent, with two candidates left, in the threshold account filed below, which records that the record leaves out ballots counted only by hand and that the state’s tabulation is conducted separately. The same account notes the arithmetic of Wednesday: the 874 write-in votes are excluded at the start of the ranked-choice process, which on its own would put her past half of the remaining first-choice votes. Certification is targeted for November 25, and results can be challenged until December 5, in the Juneau account. Settled: the governorship, by concession on Monday, and the distance—52 votes. Open: the call, which no desk has made, and whether Tuesday’s mail finds the 52 before Wednesday’s tabulation does.

Nvidia at 0400: A Petition Read at 188,548, a Board Reported Focused on Its Investigation, and the Report After the Close

The petition passed another set of readings in the night, and the board’s reported position gained a detail and kept its form: it is reported, and it is not stated. The campaign site’s public counter read 188,548 names at 5:13 p.m. Pacific on Monday, up from 181,025 at 8:13 a.m., with self-identified current employees at 9,451 and shareholders at 98,855, the affiliations unverified, in the petition account above. Against it, a person familiar with the matter said the board is not considering bringing Mr. Huang back and is not in talks about a return; the board is focused on its investigation, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton, examining his conduct and whether it compromised national security or the company’s secrets, and a British broadcaster was told the same, in the same account. The board’s only public step remains the search: a representative said on Friday it was choosing a search firm, in the same account. Mr. Gerstner, who co-signed the investors’ letter, said on Monday that he made no demands of the board, that Mr. Huang is owed a full hearing, and that the interim chief, Ms. Kress, is very capable, in the same account. The President’s Monday words stand in the same file, in both directions at once: he would not mind a comeback; he questioned the spy claim at the centre of the case—‘nobody’s proven that’—and said national security was not put at risk; and on raising the matter with President Xi he said, ‘I may,’ adding that one does not want to insult China just before arriving there. The Treasury Secretary’s position stands opposite: an outside successor and a dramatic shake-up, with answers on export compliance due within his 10 days. A prediction market puts the chance of a return at 32 percent, in the curtain account filed below. No statement from the board itself stands in the overnight file, and no finding has been made by the board, by any committee or by any court on any allegation in this file.

What the board will not say, the calendar partly answers today. The company publishes its third-quarter results at about 4:20 p.m. Eastern, with Ms. Kress’s written commentary, and holds its call at 5 p.m., at which only analysts and institutional investors may ask questions, in the accounts filed below. Consensus stands at about $108.9 billion of revenue in the backstop account filed below, roughly $109 billion in the curtain account, and $108 billion to $108.97 billion in the calls account filed below, against the company’s outlook of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2 percent, with earnings of $2.47 to $2.50 a share and a gross margin of about 74 percent in the same readings. The quarter ended on October 25, before the resignation, so the numbers will show the company Mr. Huang ran; the guidance will show the one Ms. Kress runs. Beneath the numbers stands the guarantee file: $164.5 billion of total financial commitments disclosed in the last report, the largest block up to $108.5 billion of data-centre lease guarantees, almost all of it—up to $105 billion—behind a planned campus in Ohio, signed at $105 billion and not the $250 billion first reported, in the backstop account. The shares fell 4.12 percent on Monday to $156.14 in the closing accounts, stand nearly 35 percent below their peak, and have pushed the company’s market value under $4 trillion, in the market accounts filed below. Monday’s other Washington fact stands in the same file: the Commerce Department’s interim final rule closing the route by which Chinese firms rented American computing power abroad, with licences now required for the listed countries and a 90-day clock for centres already serving them, in the curtain account.

The Markets at 0400: Seoul Below 5,000 for the First Time Since February, Brent at $91.66, and Retail Sales at 0830

Asia sold the chip stocks for a second day, and Tuesday’s session had the shape of Monday’s Wall Street correction carried east. South Korea’s Kospi declined 2.6 percent to 4,968.48, its lowest level in six months, closing below 5,000 for the first time since February, in the Press account above; Samsung Electronics fell 3.1 percent and SK Hynix 1.8 percent in that account, and 3.3 and 2.0 percent respectively in the Dow Jones account filed below—both readings are printed, as the desk found them. Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 1.3 percent to 58,860.43, with SoftBank Group down 3.9 percent in the Press account and 4.0 in the Dow Jones account, and a testing equipment maker down 4.4 percent. Taiwan’s Taiex fell 2.3 percent, its largest chip maker down 2.0; Hong Kong’s Hang Seng sank 0.9 percent to 23,539.97 and the Shanghai Composite 0.6 percent to 3,580.70, in the Press account. The session’s earlier readings stood higher, as early readings do: a regional index down 0.7 percent, the Kospi down 1.92 and the Nikkei down 1.03 in the early account filed below, and the Kospi and Taiwan down more than 2 percent each with the Nikkei down 1.2 in the Reuters account filed below. Japan’s October trade data is due Wednesday, after figures showing its economy contracted in the third quarter, in the Press account.

The American readings at 0400 are the night’s own. Futures stood little changed at midnight, in the midnight file, and in early Tuesday trading S&P 500 futures were up about 0.08 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures about 0.34 percent, in the day-ahead account filed below. Gold steadied near $3,868 an ounce after touching a one-year low near $3,830 on Monday, in the same account. Bitcoin traded near $64,500 to $64,900, above the weekend’s low near $62,000, with spot Bitcoin funds showing about $2.35 billion in net outflows over two weeks in an exchange account cited there. Oil fell through the night against the tanker file: Brent futures traded at $91.66 at 0430 GMT, down 0.8 percent, after a 3.55 percent fall on Monday to $92.44, and West Texas at $84.99, in the Brent account filed below; January contracts in the Indian morning stood at $91.67 and $83.68 in the commodities account filed below, which carries the energy agency’s November finding that global supply has passed demand for the first time since the war began. A bank’s forecast in the Brent account sees the benchmark averaging $88 in 2027 and $78 by December 2027 as the market returns to surplus.

The morning’s American fact is scheduled for 0830: October retail sales. Consensus expects a rise of about 0.2 percent on the month, down from 0.8 percent in September, with sales excluding autos up about 0.4 percent, in the preview account filed below; one bank expects 0.1 percent, held down by auto sales, with spending excluding autos and gasoline up 0.3 percent, in the same account. A retail federation’s card-based monitor has already printed its version: total spending up 0.2 percent to $561.7 billion, the slowest pace since November 2025, and core spending up 0.3 percent, in the week’s accounts. The preview account prints the caution whole: the figures are nominal, October consumer prices rose 0.4 percent, and part of any rise is prices rather than volume. Two retailers report before the open in the preview accounts. Wednesday carries the October meeting minutes; the December decision stands on December 8 and 9.

Manila at 0400: A Late-Afternoon Arrival, a Premier Already Heard, and the Quad’s First Meeting in Two Years

The President flies into the Philippines on Tuesday at the tail end of the ASEAN summit, where he could face protests, ahead of the first meeting in two years of the Quad leaders—the United States, Japan, Australia and India—in the wire account above. It will be his first Quad meeting; the last gathering of the group was two years ago, in the same account. His Tuesday, as published in the schedule account filed below, runs: arrival at Ninoy Aquino International Airport; at 6:20 p.m. he greets the Quad leaders for a photo opportunity; at 6:30, the multilateral meeting; at 7:45, an ASEAN-United States Summit Special and reception; at 8:25, a United States-ASEAN dinner. He skips the East Asia Summit, joins the special summit, signs a joint statement with Thailand’s Prime Minister on an agreement on reciprocal trade on Tuesday, and meets the Philippine President on Wednesday, in the wire account.

The room’s other case was made on Monday, before he lands. Premier Li Qiang told the ASEAN leaders on Monday that economic achievements between China and ASEAN were ‘truly extraordinary’ in the face of global trade restrictions, expressed Beijing’s commitment to free trade, and called on the region to ‘stand united, ward off interference, and work together,’ in the wire account. ASEAN’s leaders spent Tuesday in meetings with counterparts from Japan, South Korea, China and India ahead of the East Asia Summit, in the same account. The wire’s framing of the trip stands in its lede and is printed as its framing: the visit comes after the midterm defeat, with spy allegations and new American curbs on China’s access to advanced chips complicating a fragile trade truce. Settled: the arrival, the schedule, and the order of the week—Manila on Tuesday, a state visit welcome on Wednesday, Shenzhen on Thursday. Open: what the Quad says, and whether the protests the wire expects materialize.

Shenzhen at 0400: ‘Groundbreaking’ in Beijing, Four Agendas in Four Capitals, and a Fourth Chair Still Empty

Thursday’s session gained a Korean bearing in the night, and it is the bearing of the country that hosts the forum’s other business and sits closest to the fourth chair. A Seoul paper’s account, in the APEC account filed below, records that none of the parties most exposed to the agenda will be at the table—Ukraine, South Korea, or the Middle Eastern states if Iran comes up—that APEC decides by consensus and its decisions are voluntary and non-binding, and that the leaders’ meeting of November 18 and 19 puts bargaining alongside an agenda of trade, artificial intelligence and connectivity. Mr. Kim’s attendance remains uncertain in the same account: the President looks to the host to bring Mr. Kim into the lineup, and President Putin keeps a seat ready for his treaty ally, in its telling.

The agendas stand in their four versions, and the desk prints them as four. Beijing’s, from Monday’s confirmation: ‘in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations,’ in the APEC account, and ‘groundbreaking significance’ from the Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Ms. Mao Ning, in the Hong Kong account filed below. The President’s, from his departure: denuclearization, ‘tough subject because it’s very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes’; Iran, ‘in very good shape’; Ukraine, ‘my favourite subject’; and economics and trade, in the departure account filed below, which also carries his unattributed figure of 25,000 soldiers a month lost by Russia and Ukraine together. His officials’: nuclear stockpiles and Iran, a conversation to begin, no agreements expected, and Ukraine not on the trilateral agenda, in the Hong Kong account. The Kremlin’s: the meeting confirmed, no agenda stated, and a one-on-one between the President and President Putin being arranged, in the Kremlin aide’s account in the departure file—against no such meeting agreed, in the agency account carried in the Hong Kong file, and no separate meeting planned, in the White House’s earlier telling. On the fourth chair, the President’s words stand alone in the file: Mr. Kim ‘may come,’ any meeting would be in China, and ‘that’s up to President Xi’; no confirmation from Pyongyang or Beijing had accompanied the remarks, and he did not say whether an invitation had been extended, in the departure account. Before Shenzhen, the President is in Shenzhen’s host country from Wednesday for the APEC leaders’ meeting President Xi chairs.

The Gulf at 0400: A Tanker Named Off Oman, Six Sunk in a Claim and None Confirmed, and No Word on the Radar for a Third Day

The Hormuz file gained a name in the night, and the name is the night’s hardest fact in the Gulf. A British maritime agency reported a tanker attacked about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, while leaving the strait, and a security monitor identified the ship as the Panama-flagged ON PHOENIX, hit three nautical miles off Oman, in the Hormuz account filed below, which compiles a Pakistani paper, a broadcaster, a Gulf paper, the maritime agency and a strait-tracking site. It is the first vessel named in a week of claims. Against it stands Tehran’s arithmetic, grown again: six tankers caught fire and sunk since Sunday in the Guards’ claim as carried in the same account, two of them said to have struck mines on an unauthorised route, and a third tanker left immobilised after striking a mine east of the strait on Monday in the regular navy’s claim. The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved, in the same account. Tracking data showed no commercial ship had crossed the strait at all by early Tuesday morning, in the same account.

Two files in the Gulf did not move. On the radar at Al-Riffa, the overnight file adds no assessment from any capital for a third day: the Guards’ six drones and a struck radar, Manama’s intercepts, the Ambassador’s all-intercepted sentence, Friday’s two drones down in the American denial, and no impacts to American forces in the spokesman’s sentence, which did not address the machine. One aggregator’s timeline, updated Tuesday morning, carries a further claim dated Tuesday, attributed to the Guards and naming radar equipment at Sheikh Isa, in the timeline account filed below; no capital has confirmed it, and the desk prints it as a claim in a timeline and nothing more. On the inspectors, Tehran’s deputy foreign minister said on Sunday that Iran will not let United Nations inspectors visit its damaged nuclear facilities until the war ends and the United States meets its conditions, in the Hormuz account. The rest of the file stands where the week left it: three American carriers in the region, the blockade in force, the President’s words that new strikes are highly unlikely while negotiations progress, Tehran’s words that it remains in a state of war, and the Khor Mor strike unclaimed.

The Airlines at 0400: Tuesday Opens After a 344-Cancellation Monday, the Secretary Takes His Case to the Senate Republicans’ Lunch, and the Money Argument Meets at $4 Billion

Tuesday opens on the recovery’s second ordinary day, with Monday’s last reading standing at 344 cancellations and 4,800 delays by 1800 and Tuesday’s own cancellations counted at 68 in the morning’s earlier accounts, in the midnight file. Monday’s one stumble has been given its official size: the United outage was a company matter of about an hour, and ‘this is not an FAA system-wide problem,’ the Secretary said, in the AAP account filed below. No second nationwide stop stands in any account the desk read.

The money argument moved on Monday, and its two sides now cite the same small number for different purposes. The Majority Leader, Mr. Thune, said only $4 billion of the $12.5 billion approved last year had been spent, and that explanations are owed, in the accounts filed below; the Democrats’ Monday account puts the figure as spent or committed at just $4 billion, in the wire account filed with the midnight edition, against the $11 billion unspent in their earlier reading of the same appropriation. The Democratic Leader, Mr. Schumer, answered that the Administration has money, does not use it, and asks for more, and his party wants hearings into Friday’s failure, in the same accounts; Senator Schmitt answered that the funding was long overdue. The Secretary takes the case in person on Tuesday, sitting in on the Senate Republicans’ weekly lunch, in the funding account filed below, which records that as of Monday he had not released comprehensive details of how the $50 billion would be spent, that department staff will brief congressional staffers this week, and that the request now sits inside the negotiations to avoid a shutdown after December 11, when government funding runs out. The President’s sentence stands in the equipment account filed below: what the country saw on Friday was ‘very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,’ and the system should be blown up and put in new. The cause file itself gained nothing in the night: a router installed during a contractor’s copper-to-fibre work at El Dorado, a second site at Amarillo, no cyberattack in the officials’ ruling, and the root cause still unnamed. Settled: the recovery, and that both parties now argue from the unspent balance. Open: the root cause, and whether Congress pays before December 11.

France and Spain at 0400: A Strike Day Opens on the Eighth Anniversary, and a Fifth Tracking Moves the Seats Without Moving the Gap

France’s next fact is a weekday fact, and it opens today. Six union federations—the CGT, Solidaires, FSU, UNSA, CGC and FAFP—have called a nationwide strike and demonstrations for Tuesday, November 17, after the Prime Minister’s social conference, saying the government had announced only crumbs, in the week’s file; November 17 is the date the Yellow Vest movement launched in 2018, and organisers plan to mark the eighth anniversary on roundabouts and at toll booths, in the accounts filed below. The government’s wage answer stands at a 1.6 percent minimum-wage increase effective December 1, taking net monthly pay to about &euro;1,502—a &euro;24 increase the unions call too small—in the wage account filed below; earlier accounts in the file carried a 0.6 percent figure as the promise the unions rejected, and both figures are printed in the cocked hat. Saturday’s fifth day stands at 106,000 nationwide in the Interior Ministry’s count, 24,000 of them in Paris, and 200,000 in the student unions’, in the Saturday account filed below. The movement whole—from the September school blockades through the largest day, November 5, at 575,000 in the Ministry’s count and 1.6 million in the union’s—stands in the protests account filed below, which records the pan-European protests called for November 20 to 22. The police bill goes to the Senate on Thursday; a sixth Saturday is called for November 21. Settled: the strike is called, by six federations, for the anniversary. Open: its size, which Tuesday will supply.

Spain’s campaign gained a fifth daily reading in the night, and it moved the seats without moving the gap. The fifth instalment of the daily tracking puts the Popular Party at 31.8 percent, up three-tenths; the Socialists at 30.6, up three-tenths and 1.2 points past their figure at the tracking’s start; and Vox at 17.5, down half a point—with the seat projection moving against Vox alone: the Popular Party gains three seats to 133, the Socialists one to 120, and Vox loses four to 58, taking the two right parties’ combined total from 192 to 191, fifteen above the 176 needed, in the tracking account filed below. The gap between the two large parties holds at 1.2 points, and in the preference to lead the government the Socialist leader stands first at 32.8 percent, in the same account. Monday’s other polls stand apart from the tracking and from each other, in the Reuters account filed below: one projects 201 to 205 seats for the right pair and 102 to 104 for the Socialists at 26.1 percent; another puts the Socialists at 26.9 and the right bloc at 194 seats; and the state pollster stands as a major outlier, projecting 134 to 143 Socialist seats against 155 to 171 for the right. The head-to-head debate between Mr. S&aacute;nchez and Mr. Feij&oacute;o stands on Thursday, November 19; polls may publish until November 23; Spain votes on November 29.

Tuesday Opens: Sales at 0830, a Lunch, a Landing, a Count, and a Report After the Close

Tuesday carries October retail sales at 0830, the Secretary’s lunch with Senate Republicans, France’s strike day, the President’s arrival in Manila and the Quad at 1830 there, Alaska’s next count, and Nvidia’s earnings after the close. Wednesday carries the pricing of the Anthropic listing—$70 to $78 a share on 825 million shares, about $61 billion at the middle of the range in the listing account filed below, about $1.2 trillion of value at the midpoint in the same account and $1.3 to $1.45 trillion fully diluted in the test account filed below, six times oversubscribed in one report and trading in pre-listing contracts at $101.72, some 30 percent above the range’s top—the October meeting minutes, the first day of APEC in Shenzhen, Alaska’s tabulation, and Japan’s trade figures. Thursday carries the first trading day under the ticker ANT and the three presidents in Shenzhen, the police bill in the French Senate, and Spain’s debate. The Treasury Secretary’s 10 days run to about November 25, when Alaska’s certification is also targeted. Spain votes November 29; the Federal Reserve decides December 8 and 9; government funding runs out after December 11. The Midday Watch collects at 1200.

The Cocked Hat

Where the night’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Alaska: 49.98 percent on the full denominator, 50.0 rounded in the Press’s Tuesday count, 50.1 on the dashboard’s calculation in the week’s file, and 51.83 in a newspaper’s model of the scanned ballots’ final round; 52 votes short of a majority on the current total, about 6,500 ballots estimated still to count, a victory declared by one candidate, the process left to run by the other, and no call by the Press. On the petition: 180,200 in the wire’s accounts, 181,025 at 0813 Pacific on Monday, 185,600 in one evening account, and 188,548 at 1713 Pacific, the affiliations self-reported in every reading. On Nvidia’s Monday session: down 4.12 percent at $156.14 in the closing accounts, down 4.1 in the wire’s, and down 3.7 in the wire’s return account. Inside the triangle is where the week honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 34 items.

 

 SubjectiveJuneau Independent — Ms. Peltola at 49.98 percent, about 6,500 ballots estimated still to count, and Senator Sullivan’s spokesman letting the process run its courseDemocrat Mary Peltola is inching closer to an outright majority of first-choice ballots in Alaska’s Senate race, Monday’s tally giving her 49.98 percent of votes counted so far against Senator Dan S. Sullivan’s 45.93 percent, according to the Division of Elections. The Press estimates 98 percent of ballots cast have been tallied. Her lead of 4.05 percent exceeds the total of the two other candidates on the ballot, Mr. Heikes at 2.12 percent and Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan at 1.65 percent. Monday’s tally includes 874 write-in votes, which would be excluded at the beginning of the ranked-choice process if it becomes necessary on Wednesday. The tally is for 285,439 ballots, 47.15 percent of registered voters; NBC News estimates about 6,500 ballots remain to be counted. Senator Sullivan’s spokesman, Mr. Adams, said Monday night that Alaskans deserve a complete and accurate count and the campaign will let the process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified, that it will not comment on individual ballot updates or outside projections, and that the campaign will have more to say by the end of the week. The Division is scheduled to certify the election on November 25, and results can be challenged in court until December 5.

 SubjectiveNewsPub — Saturday’s threshold arithmetic, and an independent tabulation of the scanned ballots that puts Ms. Peltola at 51.83 percent in the final roundMs. Peltola is just 157 votes short of an outright majority on Saturday’s figures: the Division’s unofficial summary released Saturday afternoon showed her with 140,637 first-choice votes, 49.94 percent, to Senator Sullivan’s 129,424, 45.96 percent, with Mr. Heikes at 6,002, Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 4,652 and 872 write-ins. A candidate who wins more than half of first-choice votes is elected outright; if no one does, the Division begins a ranked-choice tabulation on November 18, and ballots mailed from overseas can still arrive through November 18. A newspaper independently ran the Division’s ballot-level cast vote record, covering 282,698 scanned ballots, through open-source tabulation software with settings matching the Division’s published rules: with two candidates left, 276,112 ballots were still active, and the model showed Ms. Peltola with 143,127 votes, 51.83 percent, to Senator Sullivan’s 132,985, 48.16 percent, a lead of 10,142. That is the newspaper’s independent model of the scanned ballots, not the state’s official result; the Division’s record leaves out ballots counted only by hand, and the state’s official tabulation will be conducted separately.

 SubjectiveThe Curtain — Nvidia faces investors without Mr. Huang as Washington closes the chip loopholeNvidia will report quarterly results on Tuesday in the strangest circumstances of its history: record-breaking numbers, a missing founder, and a government in Washington that has just rewritten the rules for the company’s most important market. The company releases its third-quarter results after the market closes, at about 4:20 p.m. Eastern, followed by an earnings call at 5 p.m.—its first since Mr. Huang resigned as chief executive on November 12, ending a 33-year run as the only chief executive the company has ever had. The interim chief, Ms. Kress, the company’s finance chief of 13 years, will lead the call, with the board still searching for a permanent successor. Analysts expect revenue of roughly $109 billion, against the company’s own guidance of $108 billion, and earnings of $2.47 a share. The quarter ended on October 25, before Mr. Huang’s departure, so the results will show what the company delivered under his leadership. The wire, citing anonymous sources, has reported that the board is not considering bringing Mr. Huang back, despite a public campaign that has gathered more than 180,200 signatures and Mr. Musk’s backing. Mr. Huang resigned amid revelations about two extramarital relationships, one with an executive who reported to him, and reports that American intelligence officials said this spring that a former executive at the Singapore-based computing business Megaspeed was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security—a claim China has denied. The Treasury Secretary has demanded that the board and its outside lawyers answer within ten days whether the company built a corporate culture of complying with export controls, and has said the next chief executive should be recruited from outside. On Monday, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule closing the loophole that let Chinese firms rent American computing power abroad. A prediction market puts the chance of Mr. Huang rejoining the company at 32 percent. What happens next comes fast: the earnings call on Tuesday evening, the board’s ten-day deadline to answer the Treasury Secretary, and a 90-day clock for data-centre operators to comply with the new rule.

The Ohio guarantee is signed at $105 billion, not $250 billion, and the underwriting standard now requires binding offtake. A reinstatement would not restore the terms that existed in July, and would have to clear an independent investigation, a board that has retained outside counsel, and a Congress now examining the China dimension of the case. Two investors have asked the board to keep the search slow and consider all leadership options including Mr. Huang’s return—the language of investors preserving an option, not of a board preparing a reversal.

 SubjectiveTradingKey — the October retail sales preview: consensus at 0.2 percent, one bank at 0.1, and the prices inside the salesOn November 17, Eastern Time, the United States will release the latest retail sales data for October. Consensus estimates project headline retail sales to rise by about 0.2 percent month over month in October, down significantly from 0.8 percent in September, while retail sales excluding autos are expected to increase by roughly 0.4 percent. One bank’s economists expect headline retail sales to grow by just 0.1 percent, dragged down primarily by a slowdown in auto sales, though spending excluding autos and gasoline is still forecast to rise by 0.3 percent, indicating that consumer fundamentals retain some support. High-frequency data from a retail federation also showed that retail sales excluding autos and gasoline continued to post positive growth in October. The data also needs to be evaluated in the context of inflation: retail sales measure nominal sales and do not adjust for price changes, and with October consumer prices rising 0.4 percent month over month and core prices up 0.3 percent, part of the sales growth may stem from higher prices rather than increases in real consumption volume.

The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved. Tracking data showed no commercial ship had crossed the strait at all by early Tuesday morning. A United Nations maritime body has recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the strait and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11, including 35 in October alone. The third carrier arrived on Sunday. The Guards also claimed responsibility for targeting an American radar installation at the Riffa base in Bahrain with six drones. Iran will not let United Nations inspectors visit its damaged nuclear facilities until the war ends and the United States meets its conditions, the deputy foreign minister, Mr. Gharibabadi, said in a televised interview on Sunday. The account’s sources are listed as a Pakistani paper, a broadcaster, a Gulf paper, the British maritime agency and a strait-tracking site.

 SubjectiveWorldAttention — the timeline of the exchanges in Bahrain and the strait, updated Tuesday, with the claims and the denials in sequenceIran’s Guards said it launched six drones at an American air defence radar facility at the al-Riffa base in Bahrain on Sunday, describing the attack as retaliation. Bahrain’s military said its air defences intercepted and destroyed the attacks before they reached their targets, and the interior ministry urged residents to seek shelter. It was the second Iranian drone attack on Bahrain in three days; the American military denied an earlier claim of hitting a radar facility on Friday, saying two drones were shot down with no damage. The strikes further undermined stalled diplomacy over the strait. The summary, updated on the morning of November 17, covers the current reports; its timeline carries a further claim dated Tuesday, attributed to the Guards, identifying the target as American radar equipment at a Bahraini facility at Sheikh Isa. Iran claimed a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait, though there was no independent verification. The account’s own assessment is printed with it: the verifiable story is the mining of the strait and the threat to commercial shipping, and the radar claim should stay in the headline as an open question, not be treated as a confirmed event.

 SubjectiveAAP — the transport chief says the United glitch is isolated and not a system-wide problem, and $4 billion of the $12.5 billion spent in the Majority Leader’s figureThe latest technological glitch to hit the United States’ aviation sector is not a system-wide problem, the Transportation Secretary says. Air travel was brought to a standstill on Friday, when the Administration grounded all departing flights nationwide after a communications failure hit air traffic control centres across the country. It was the second such action since the September 11 attacks in 2001 and the longest ground stop in 25 years, with more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days. By Monday night, the network had largely returned to normal, but the resumption was briefly marred by a United Airlines technology outage. Calls are mounting for more investment in air traffic control systems. ‘This is not an FAA system-wide problem,’ the Secretary said of the United outage. As the turmoil unfolded on Friday, the Secretary raised his request for funding for air traffic control and airports to $50 billion, from $30 billion previously. The Administration is still using aging equipment including Compaq computers, floppy disks, 25-year-old obsolete routers and paper strips to track aircraft. The President agreed funding was needed to upgrade the air traffic control system. While $12.5 billion had already been approved by Congress to improve the systems, only $4 billion had been spent to date, the Senate Majority Leader said.

 SubjectiveUSA Today — ground stop chaos spurs a fight in Congress over funding: the Secretary at the Senate Republicans’ lunch on November 17, and no comprehensive details yetCongress is under pressure to act after air traffic control issues grounded flights nationwide last week, setting up a new funding fight on Capitol Hill and further complicating lawmakers’ efforts to avoid another government shutdown before Christmas. Administration officials are pleading for billions of additional dollars to modernize what they acknowledge is an aging system. The Transportation Secretary said he is asking lawmakers to fast-track a $50 billion package to prevent further communications malfunctions like the one that derailed air travel before the weekend. The new funding request could quickly become another variable in the ongoing negotiations to avoid another shutdown after December 11, when government funding is set to run out. The meltdown was caused by a breakdown in the communications network, prompted by the replacement of a router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, as part of an ongoing effort to switch out old copper wires with fiber-optic cable. The President weighed in on the situation for the first time on November 16. The Secretary is expected to sit in on Senate Republicans’ weekly lunch on November 17, where he will continue to make the case for his funding request. As of November 16, he had not released comprehensive details on how the $50 billion request would be spent. Transportation Department and Administration staff will brief congressional staffers about the latest funding request this week.

 SubjectiveThe Hindu BusinessLine — the President blames ageing equipment: ‘very, very old equipment that had a heart attack’The President has urged Congress to approve billions of dollars to replace the country’s ageing air traffic control network. He blamed Friday’s rare nationwide ground stop on ageing aviation infrastructure, saying ‘very, very old equipment had a heart attack,’ as he renewed pressure on Congress to approve billions of dollars to completely replace the network. Addressing the hours-long flight freeze that cancelled more than 9,100 flights and stranded travellers nationwide, he argued that decades of underinvestment had left the United States relying on obsolete hardware that needs to be torn out rather than patched. ‘We have old equipment, broken equipment. We’ve been telling that to Congress,’ he said. ‘We essentially want to blow it up and put new in. We need the funding to get it done.’ Friday’s incident, only the second nationwide ground stop since 2001, stemmed from a telecommunications and router overload triggered while a contractor was replacing legacy copper wiring with fibre-optic lines at remote sites in Arkansas and Texas. Transportation officials ruled out any cyberattack or artificial intelligence involvement.

 SubjectiveNutshell Today — more than 100,000 rally nationwide on Saturday, and another nationwide strike planned for November 17More than 100,000 people took to the streets across France on November 14, as students, workers and trade unions continued protests over education standards, living costs, low wages and police violence. With another nationwide strike planned for November 17, the demonstrations are adding to pressure on the government. The Interior Ministry estimated that 106,000 people joined Saturday’s protests, including 24,000 in Paris; student unions put the nationwide turnout at 200,000. Trade unions have called another nationwide strike for November 17, rejecting the government’s proposed minimum wage increase as ‘crumbs.’ The November 17 strike will coincide with the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, which began in 2018 over rising fuel prices and grew into a wider challenge to the government’s economic policies and the cost of living.

 SubjectiveNewzino — France brings forward a minimum wage increase of 1.6 percent to December 1, at about &euro;1,502 net a month, and the unions call &euro;24 too smallFrance will raise its minimum wage by 1.6 percent on December 1, taking net monthly pay to about &euro;1,502, after more than two months of protests over the cost of living. Unions called the &euro;24 increase too small and are staging a day of action on November 17. In the account’s timeline: on November 9 the unions rejected the increase as too small—one federation’s leader calls it crumbs in the wider file—and the federation called a new protest for November 17. A prediction market’s question is printed with the account: if other major unions join and schools or transport close for a full day, the protest wave would move beyond student-led demonstrations and become a broader challenge to the government before the election.

 Subjectivepolitical.org — France’s protests whole: the movement from the school blockades to the November 17 strike call, and the counts of the largest daysA protest movement that began in late September with students angry about underfunded schools has grown into a nationwide challenge to the government, producing some of the worst street violence in years. The movement began among high school and university students in Paris protesting poor school conditions, teacher shortages and infrastructure problems. The largest single day of protest, Thursday, November 5, drew 575,000 people by the Interior Ministry’s count and 1.6 million by the union’s. On Monday, November 9, the Prime Minister announced a 1.6 percent minimum-wage increase effective December 1; the unions rejected it. Public-sector unions have called a strike and demonstrations for Tuesday, November 17, and some groups have called for pan-European protests from November 20 to 22. The unrest first began in late September. The turning point came on Saturday, October 17. That day’s demonstrations were organized by the coalition of France’s main unions, with students and the Yellow Vest movement joining. France has a long record of street movements that start over a single grievance and widen; the 2018 protests began on November 17 in opposition to rising fuel taxes and swelled into a movement against the President and the biggest challenge of his presidency. The current wave combines union-led strikes, student mobilization and Yellow Vest participation, and is part of a broader wave of discontent across Europe, with young people in several countries staging similar protests in recent weeks.

 SubjectiveDem&oacute;crata — the fifth daily tracking: the Popular Party at 31.8 percent and 133 seats, the Socialists at 30.6 and 120, Vox down four seats to 58, and the combined right at 191The general election poll by the tracking firm for a national newspaper and a radio network on November 17 places the Popular Party at 31.8 percent of the vote and the Socialists at 30.6 percent. Both parties advance three-tenths compared to Monday, while Vox retreats half a point, to 17.5 percent. The gap between the conservatives and the socialists remains 1.2 points. The most pronounced change appears in the seats: Vox loses four deputies and stands at 58; the Popular Party gains three and reaches 133, including the two from its Navarre partner, while the Socialists add one and reach 120. The combined projection for the two right parties goes from 192 to 191 deputies, 15 above the 176 needed for an absolute majority. Since the first installment, published on November 13, the Socialists have moved from 29.4 percent to 30.6 percent, an increase of 1.2 points; in the same period the Popular Party goes from 31.5 to 31.8. The Socialists have cut nine-tenths off the distance compared to the start of daily tracking. In the preference to lead the government, the Socialist leader stands at 32.8 percent of those surveyed, the Popular leader at 22.2 and the Vox leader at 17.3; those figures measure presidential preference and do not equate to the vote estimate.

 SubjectiveReuters — Spain’s right retains a firm poll lead despite Socialist gains: three polls on Monday, and the state pollster a major outlierMADRID, November 16 (Reuters) — Spain’s conservative People’s Party and Vox would together win a parliamentary majority in the November 29 election, three opinion polls published on Monday showed, though the Prime Minister’s Socialists gained ground. The surveys are the first since last week’s campaign launch, which has focused on housing affordability, immigration, corruption and last month’s deadly train crash. A daily poll showed the Socialists rising to 30.3 percent from 29.9, exceeding the 30 percent mark for the first time in that poll since the 2023 election, with the Popular Party on 31.5 and Vox on 18, together winning more than 190 seats in the 350-seat lower house. A second poll projected 201 to 205 seats for the two right parties combined and 102 to 104 for the Socialists, whose support rose half a point to 26.1 percent. A third showed Socialist support up one point from a week earlier to 26.9 percent, with the right bloc winning 194 seats to the Socialists’ 109. The state pollster remained a major outlier: last week it projected 134 to 143 seats for the Socialists against 155 to 171 for the two right parties combined, suggesting the Prime Minister could retain power through a broad left-wing coalition.

 SubjectiveEuronews, carried by Ekkow — five things to know before Anthropic goes public: pricing on Wednesday, trading on Thursday under ANT, at $70 to $78 a shareThe company will launch an initial public offering on November 19. It is expected to set the final price of its shares on Wednesday, November 18, and begin trading on an exchange in New York the following day under the symbol ANT. The company has proposed a price of $70 to $78 a share, which would value it at about $1.2 trillion in the middle of that range. The listing will be the biggest test yet of whether investors believe artificial intelligence can make money over the long term. Not everyone is convinced: at a briefing organised by an investor-responsibility centre, governance and legal experts warned of ‘red flags’ in the company’s filings, and a New York City financial officer said the company is rushing toward a listing without answering fundamental questions about its readiness to operate as a publicly traded company. The filing shows a large technology company and a search company’s parent among its largest backers. In May, the company raised $65 billion from investors who valued it at $965 billion, the first time a funding round had valued it above its rival. It is offering 825 million shares to the public at $70 to $78 each; at the middle of the price range, that would raise roughly $61 billion, making it one of the largest listings ever. The company is a public benefit corporation, legally required to pursue a stated purpose as well as profit. It has committed to spend at least $518 billion with six suppliers over roughly a decade, to secure the chips, data centres and electricity its models need. Its direct competitor has pushed its own listing back to 2027 at the earliest and was recently valued at about $1.25 trillion in a private round, according to reports.

 SubjectiveOANDA — the listing as a make-or-break test: six times oversubscribed in one report, $900.9 billion in commitments, and a pre-listing contract at $101.72The listing has reportedly attracted demand equivalent to approximately six times the shares available, according to a financial wire’s report published on Thursday, November 12. At the upper end of its indicative $70 to $78 price range, the company is seeking to raise approximately $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares, potentially valuing the company at around $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The offering is expected to be priced on Wednesday, November 18, ahead of its anticipated trading debut under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19. These dates remain subject to the final offering timetable. According to its amended registration statement dated November 10, the company disclosed approximately $900.9 billion in aggregate computing and infrastructure commitments over multiple years, including $451.6 billion expected through 2030, and approximately $146.6 billion in available liquidity as of September 30. Its third-quarter revenue reached approximately $17 billion, an increase of 47 percent quarter on quarter, compared with growth of 144 percent recorded in the second quarter. Based on the current price of $101.72 of its pre-listing perpetual futures on a per-share basis, at the time of writing, it is trading at around a 30 percent premium to the upper end of the expected $78.00 price.

### Monday Closes With Alaska at 52 Votes From a Majority and Its Governorship Conceded, the Airlines at 344 Cancelled With a United Outage Inside the Recovery, the Board Reported by Three Voices Not Weighing Mr. Huang's Return on the Night Before Earnings, and Futures Little Changed With the President Airborne for Manila

Filed as: Edition No. 57 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-17T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-17-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Monday Closes With Alaska at 52 Votes From a Majority and Its Governorship Conceded, the Airlines at 344 Cancelled With a United Outage Inside the Recovery, the Board Reported by Three Voices Not Weighing Mr. Huang’s Return on the Night Before Earnings, and Futures Little Changed With the President Airborne for Manila

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a count that moved after three days standing still and stopped 52 votes short of the line that ends it; a governorship conceded in the same report; a recovery that held at 344 cancelled and stumbled once, inside one airline, for about an hour; a board whose position is now carried by three voices and still not by the board; a market that fell into a correction by day and stood still by night; and a president in the air between Washington and Manila, with Thursday’s room in Shenzhen still described four ways.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Tuesday, November 17, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 56, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Monday, in Edition No. 55, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Monday, in Edition No. 54, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Monday, and in Edition No. 53, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Monday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Monday Settled, What It Left Open

Monday settled the recovery, the shape of the funding fight, and the distance left in Alaska—52 votes—and it left open the root cause of Friday’s stop, the condition of the radar at Al-Riffa, the board’s own word from Nvidia, and the call in Alaska, which is now a matter of arithmetic and one more day of mail. Alaska’s count moved in the state’s report timed 1713 on Monday, in the Alaska account filed below: Ms. Peltola at 141,637 votes and Senator Sullivan at 130,162, and Ms. Wilson’s concession in the governor’s race in the same account. The airlines’ last reading stands at 344 cancellations and 4,800 delays by 1800, with a United outage of about an hour resolved by 1800, in the updated wire account filed below. Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return, three people told the wire, in the return account filed below, and the company reports on Tuesday. Futures stood little changed on Monday night, in the night account filed below. The desk takes the files in that order.

Alaska at Midnight: A Count That Moved 1,821 Ballots, a Lead of 11,475, and 52 Votes to the Line

The count that spent Sunday and Monday morning where Saturday left it moved on Monday afternoon, and it moved toward the line without reaching it. The Division of Elections’ latest unofficial report, timestamped 5:13 p.m. Monday, shows 285,439 ballots counted, an increase of 1,821 from Saturday’s report, with turnout at 47.15 percent of registered voters, in the Alaska account above. In the Senate race Ms. Peltola has 141,637 votes, or 49.98 percent, against Senator Sullivan’s 130,162, or 45.93 percent; she added 1,000 votes in the update and he added 738, and her lead grew from 11,213 to 11,475, in the same account. On the report’s total of 283,377 votes in the contest, a majority is 141,689, and Ms. Peltola stands 52 votes short of it—against 157 short on Saturday’s figures, in the majority account filed below. The threshold rises as more ballots are counted, in the Alaska account; more ballots arriving by mail will be counted on Tuesday, and overseas ballots may arrive through Wednesday, when the ranked-choice tabulation is run for the races that need it, in the same account. The Press has not called the race, in the markets account filed below, whose last reading before the update stood at Saturday’s numbers. Mr. Heikes stands at 6,020 votes and Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 4,684, with 874 write-ins, in the Alaska account.

The same report settled the state’s other large race. Ms. Wilson said she called Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins to congratulate him on his win in the governor’s race, in the Alaska account; the Kreiss-Tomkins and Johnson ticket stands at 142,591 votes, or 50.93 percent, above the first-round threshold if the majority holds, against 78,305 for the Wilson and Shower ticket, in the same account. In the House race Mr. Begich leads Mr. Hill 134,456 to 117,607 and remains below a first-round majority at 47.67 percent, in the same account. Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal ranked-choice voting, is losing, 145,133 no votes to 125,303 yes, and Ballot Measure 3, on voter citizenship qualifications, is passing, in the same account. Settled: the governorship, by concession, and the Senate arithmetic at 52. Open: the call, Tuesday’s mail, and Wednesday’s tabulation if the 52 are not found first.

The Airlines at Midnight: 344 Cancelled by 1800, a United Outage of About an Hour, and New Figures in the Funding Fight

Monday’s recovery held to the end of the day, and its last count in the file is the evening count. By 6 p.m. Eastern there were 344 flight cancellations and 4,800 delays, down from more than 2,300 cancelled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday, in the updated wire account above; the day’s series stands at 55 cancelled as of Sunday evening, about 250 by 0400, 533 by 0700, 300 by 0900, 330 by 1330 and 344 by 1800—readings at different hours on different bases, agreeing that the day ran in the hundreds against the thousands of each of the three days before it, which together stand at more than 18,000 cancellations. Inside the recovery, one airline stumbled on its own: United experienced a technology outage affecting its departing flights for about an hour on Monday, resolved by 6 p.m. Eastern and affecting no other airline, and by 6:50 p.m. United had delayed 645 flights, or 20 percent of its schedule, and cancelled 25, in the same account; how many of those were caused by the outage and how many by the recovery from Friday’s stop was unclear, in the same account. No second nationwide stop was ordered on Monday in any account the desk read. Tuesday’s cancellations stood at 68 due to be cancelled, in the morning’s accounts.

The funding fight gained figures from both parties on Monday, and the figures do not meet. Senate Majority Leader Thune said on Monday that only $4 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress to improve air traffic control systems had been spent, and that explanations are owed for why the number is where it is, in the updated wire account; he said that just $12 billion of the larger sum sought was for air traffic modernisation, with the remainder for airport-related projects, in the same account. Senate Democratic Leader Schumer said on Monday that the Administration has money, does not use it, and then comes back and asks for more, in the same account; the Democrats’ figure in the day’s earlier accounts was $11 billion of the $12.5 billion unspent, in the funding account in the evening file, and Representative DeLauro’s sentence stands there: a $50 billion ransom without a real plan. Senator Schmitt answered for the other side that the funding was long overdue and the can has been kicked for a long time, in the updated wire account. The Secretary’s words stand in the same account: “This rickety system is telegraphing to the American people, ‘Hey, we need investment.’ Now is the time to do a big dollar amount to modernize the system.” The President’s sentence stands there too: what the country saw on Friday was very old equipment that had a heart attack. The brokerage estimate of the weekend’s cost to the four largest airlines stands at $345 million, and the Secretary’s estimate of the broader impact in the billions, in the same accounts. The Secretary sits in on the Senate Republicans’ weekly lunch on Tuesday to make the case, and the Democrats want hearings into what led to Friday’s disruption, in the updated wire account. Settled: the recovery, and that both parties now argue from the unspent balance. Open: the root cause, which no account on Monday supplied, and whether Congress pays.

Nvidia at Midnight: Three Voices Against a Return, a Tower Lit in Taipei, and Earnings on Tuesday

The board’s position gained a third voice on Monday and kept its form: it is reported, and it is not stated. Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Mr. Huang as chief executive, three people told the wire, in the return account above; one of them said, “The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back.” No statement from the board itself, from the company, or from the interim chief, Ms. Kress, stands in the midnight file. The campaign’s counter in the same account stands at more than 180,200 signatures, with more than 8,800 signatories identifying themselves as current employees and more than 94,000 as shareholders, the affiliations self-reported and unverified, in the same account and in the agenda account filed below. Taipei 101, Taiwan’s tallest building, was illuminated on Monday with messages including “Taiwan Loves Jensen,” in the return account. The President said on Monday that he would not mind seeing Mr. Huang reinstated and that “I think he learned a big lesson,” in the same account, which also carries a newspaper’s review of his financial disclosures putting his holdings in the company at between $13 million and $62 million as of the end of August. Mr. Bessent’s position stands where Sunday put it: an outside successor and a dramatic shake-up, in the same account. Mr. Altman, asked on Monday at a public event in San Francisco whether Mr. Huang should return, said he did not have enough information to answer, and said the demand for artificial intelligence would hold up, in the Altman account filed below. The intelligence question inside the file stands in the return account at its reported width: agencies are still trying to determine the extent of the relationship in question, and evidence gathered so far indicates an intelligence asset rather than a fully trained spy, two sources said; no finding by the board, by any committee, or by any court on any allegation in this file has been made, and the desk prints the allegations as allegations.

What the board will not say, the calendar will partly answer on Tuesday. The company reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday at about 4:20 p.m. Eastern, with a call at 5 p.m. led by Ms. Kress, in the accounts filed below; consensus revenue stands at about $109 billion in the week’s readings, against the company’s outlook of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2 percent, and earnings per share at $2.47, in the preview account filed below, which puts the options market’s expected move at 8.6 percent in either direction. The shares fell 4.12 percent to $156.14 in the closing accounts, in the evening file, and 3.7 percent on Monday in the return account—two readings of the same session, printed apart in the cocked hat below. The stock has lost $735 billion in market value since the scandal broke, in the follow account filed below. The Commerce Department’s rule, the Administration’s first policy answer, stands where the evening file printed it: licences for advanced chips going to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, licences for data centres above 12 million in total processing performance that serve companies headquartered in China and other listed countries, 90 days for centres already serving them, and the January 2025 diffusion rule rescinded, in the rule account and the loophole account filed below. Settled: the board is not weighing a return, on three voices. Open: the board’s own word, and Tuesday’s numbers.

The Markets at Midnight: A Correction by Day, Little Changed by Night, and Asia Lower on Tuesday

Monday’s closes stand where the evening file printed them, and the night added stillness, not a turn. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.49 percent to 24,509.76 and stands in a correction, more than 10 percent below its October 6 high; the S&P 500 fell 1.92 percent to 7,416.59; the Dow fell 739.38 points, or 1.41 percent, to 51,608.17; the semiconductor index fell 5.28 percent, in the evening file. Stock futures were little changed on Monday night after the losing session: Dow futures inched up 8 points, or 0.02 percent, S&P 500 futures were up 0.06 percent, and Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.1 percent, in the night account above. Asia-Pacific markets opened lower on Tuesday: Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.76 percent and the Topix declined 1.06 percent at the open, in the same account. Asian equities fell on Tuesday morning as the Commerce Department’s rule added to the concerns over the artificial intelligence trade, in the Asia account filed below, which reckons the rule’s first day erased an estimated $960 billion in American technology market capitalisation. Chairman Warsh’s Monday speech stands settled as the day’s set piece: three staff scenarios for the technology he calls super intelligence—shared gains, displacement, and disappointed returns—illustrative scenarios, not forecasts, no rate proposed and no guidance given, in the wire account filed below; the external task forces’ recommendations are due around the end of the year, in the accounts filed below. The October meeting minutes are published on Wednesday, and the December decision stands on December 8 and 9. Settled: the correction, and a quiet night. Open: Tuesday’s retail sales at 0830 and Nvidia after the close, which every account in the file names as the week’s deciding facts.

The President’s Road at Midnight: Airborne for Manila, a Premier Already in the Room, and a Word Changed on the Spying Matter

The President is in the air, and the room he lands in has been sitting since the weekend. He departed Washington on Monday for Manila, where the ASEAN summit opened over the weekend and sits through Tuesday, and continues to Shenzhen for the APEC meeting and Thursday’s session of the three presidents, in the accounts in the evening file. In Manila on Monday, Premier Li Qiang opened China’s case to the regional leaders: at a time of growing unilateralism and protectionism, he said, economic relations between China and ASEAN had only strengthened, and he called the ties extraordinary, in the Manila account filed below, which records that the President is due to arrive on Tuesday at the tail end of the summit, that protests are expected in Manila, and that his first meeting of the Quad—the United States, Japan, Australia and India—is the first such gathering in two years. One word of his Monday remarks changed a file the desk has carried since Friday. The President said on Monday that he “might” bring up the spying matter with President Xi, in the trip account filed below; American officials had previously said they did not expect him to start those conversations, and the midday file carried officials saying the President does not intend to raise it, in the same contrast. The rest of the agenda file stands in its four versions, printed in the evening edition and unamended at midnight: Ukraine on the table in the President’s own words and off it in his officials’; nuclear arms and Iran in Washington’s telling; world peace and strategic stability in Beijing’s; a separate meeting with President Putin beyond doubt in the Kremlin aide’s account and not planned in the White House’s; and a fourth leader, Mr. Kim, who may come, at the host’s invitation, in the departure account and the road account filed below. Europe’s seat stands where the evening file left it: no agreement reached on Europeans joining the talks, in Mr. Ushakov’s Monday words, and a clear signal from the Europeans required first, in the condition account in the evening file. Settled: the departure, and the host’s confirmation of Thursday. Open: the agenda, the fourth chair, and whether the spying matter is raised.

The Gulf and France at Midnight: No New Word on the Radar, and a Strike Day Opening in France

The radar file gained no new word on Monday, and at midnight the desk records a second day of silence as a fact of the file. The file stands whole in the explainer account filed below: six drones targeted the radar at Al-Riffa in the Guards’ claim; several attacks intercepted and destroyed in Manama’s account; all drones intercepted in the Ambassador’s Sunday sentence; two drones shot down in Friday’s denial, which concerned Friday’s claim; no impacts to American forces in the Central Command spokesman’s sentence, which did not address the radar; and no assessment of the radar’s condition from any capital, in any account the desk read on Monday. The rest of the Gulf file stands where the week left it: three American carriers in the region in a force of more than 20 ships, the President’s words that new strikes are highly unlikely while negotiations progress, Tehran’s words that Iran remains in a state of war, and the Khor Mor strike unclaimed.

France’s next fact is a weekday fact, and it opens on Tuesday. The unions have called a new day of strikes and demonstrations for Tuesday, November 17, in the strike account filed below: the CGT, Solidaires, FSU, UNSA, CGC and FAFP federations called the day after the Prime Minister’s social conference, saying the government had announced only crumbs, and November 17 is the date the Yellow Vest movement launched in 2018, in the same account. The wider European week stands in the protests account filed below: a European youth strike called for November 20 across six countries, an Italian strike day the same day, and protests called in Lisbon and Brussels. Saturday’s French counts stand at 106,000 nationwide in the Interior Ministry’s and about 200,000 in the organisers’, with 219 detained, in the week’s file; the police bill is examined by the Senate on Thursday, and a sixth Saturday is called for November 21. Spain’s calendar stands: a head-to-head debate reported for Thursday, polls publishable until November 23, and the vote on November 29. Settled: the strike is called, by six federations, for the anniversary. Open: its size, which Tuesday will supply.

Tuesday at Midnight: The Week’s Calendar Is Now the File’s Largest Settled Fact

Tuesday carries October retail sales at 0830, the Secretary’s lunch with Senate Republicans, France’s strike day, the President’s arrival in Manila, Alaska’s next count, and Nvidia’s earnings after the close. Wednesday carries the October meeting minutes, the first day of APEC in Shenzhen, Alaska’s tabulation, and Anthropic’s pricing. Thursday carries the three presidents in Shenzhen, the police bill in the French Senate, Spain’s debate, and Anthropic’s first trading day in New York. The Treasury Secretary’s 10 days for answers on export compliance run to about November 25, when Alaska’s certification is also targeted. Spain votes on November 29; the Federal Reserve decides on December 8 and 9; government funding runs out after December 11. The Overnight Watch collects at 0400.

The Cocked Hat

Where the midnight’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Alaska: 49.98 percent on the state’s full denominator in Monday’s report and 50.1 percent on the dashboard’s calculation in the week’s file, 52 votes short of a majority on the current total and a winner listed on one tracker, a victory declared by Ms. Peltola and no call by the Press. On the money for the air system: $4 billion of the $12.5 billion spent in the Majority Leader’s Monday figure, $11 billion unspent in the Democrats’, $1 billion spent in an earlier Democratic reading, $50 billion asked, $12 billion of the larger ask for modernisation in the Majority Leader’s account, and a ransom without a plan in Representative DeLauro’s. On the day’s flights: 55 cancelled as of Sunday evening, about 250 by 0400, 533 by 0700, 300 by 0900, 330 by 1330 and 344 by 1800, and on United’s own day, 645 delayed and 25 cancelled at 1850 with the outage’s share of them unclear. On Nvidia’s session: down 4.12 percent at $156.14 in the closing accounts and down 3.7 percent in the wire’s return account. On the board: a return discussed with confidants in the Sunday report, a return not weighed in Monday’s three voices, a president who would not mind it and who holds the stock, an investor who never heard of it from the man himself, a Treasury Secretary set against it, and a petition counted at 168,000, 180,000, 180,200 and 185,600 at four hours across two days. On Shenzhen: Ukraine on the agenda in the President’s words and off it in his officials’, the spying matter not to be raised in the officials’ telling and maybe raised in the President’s, no separate meeting in the White House’s account and a meeting beyond doubt in the Kremlin aide’s. On the radar: six drones on target, several attacks destroyed, all drones intercepted, two drones down on Friday, no impacts to forces, and no word on the machine, for a second day. On France: 106,000 in the Ministry’s Saturday count and about 200,000 in the organisers’. Inside the triangle is where the day honestly stands, and the log turns on it.
